To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the risk of a claim following THA was lower among male patients, those with cemented prostheses, and those operated on at hospitals with an intermediate volume of operations, and higher among patients with comorbidity, while the risk following TKA was higher among patients with increased comorbidities and lower among patients operated on at hospitals performing more than 300 operations.
patients over 65 are less likely to file claims and receive compensation than patients under 60.
the risk of malpractice claims and compensations after THA and T KA is associated with patient age, gender, comorbidity and prosthesis type.
In summary, our research is concerned with
factors associated with malpractice in a no-fult system.
the factors that predispose to claims and compensable injuries in THA and T KA.
patient characteristics that may predispose to claims and compensable injuries, and hospital characteristics that may affect the likelihood of a patient filing a claim and receiving compensation.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results of this study should not be used as a reason for centralization of THA and T KA.
centralization of TKA and increased attention to the equal treatment of patients in a no-fauls scheme are needed.
the factors predisposing to claims for injuries following THA are different from those predisposing to claims following TKA.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
centralization of high-volume procedures, such as TKA, to a limited number of hospitals may reduce the rate and severity of patient injuries.
patient characteristics, such as comorbidity and age, are associated with claims, while hospital characteristics, such as volume, are associated with compensations.
patient characteristics, such as age and sex, and prosthesis type affect the probability of filing a claim.
